brief.topic: Why Averaging Predictions Can Reduce Squared Error

s01: Two models predict one and three. The correct answer is two.
Their squared errors are both one. But their average prediction is exactly right.
Draw squared error as a curve over the prediction.
Join the two predictions on that curve. The middle of the joining line gives their average loss.
The curve below gives the loss of their average prediction. It cannot be higher.
For any two predictions, the gap is one quarter of their squared difference.
The correct answer cancels out of this gap. This comparison holds for any target.
This is a two point example of convexity, and Jensen's inequality.
It explains one benefit of averaging model outputs under squared error.
It compares with the average loss, not necessarily with the better model.
Now let the correct answer be one instead.
The first model is perfect. The average prediction has squared error one.
It still beats the average loss of two, but it does not beat the best model. An exact guarantee can be useful without promising everything.
